_comment: EVERY NUMBER IN THIS FILE IS AN ESTIMATE until a --meter run proves it, and treating one as fact is listed under 'Common mistakes' in CLAUDE.md. This is the money path: a credit is the unit a customer is charged in, so a wrong number here is not a wrong render, it is a wrong invoice. Nothing in scripts/auth/ hardcodes any of it -- one metered run has to be able to correct all of it in one edit, which is only true if there is exactly one copy. It supersedes config/pricing.json's `fal/video-UNVERIFIED` guess ($0.20/second, $3.00 per 15s) with a published formula plus a ratio, which is better evidence and still not a measurement.
_creditUSD_comment: ESTIMATE. What one credit is worth in ESTIMATED PROVIDER COST, and therefore the only thing that converts dollars into the unit on the button. Ten cents is a round, explainable number rather than a derived one, and it is a scale factor and nothing else: it is NOT the price a credit is sold at, and no code in scripts/auth/ multiplies it by anything a customer pays. Change it and every credit figure below moves together, which is the point. RAISED FROM $0.03 ON 2026-08-21, at Paul's direction, and the reason was legibility rather than economics: at three cents a tape cost 51 or 152 credits, which are ugly numbers that read as arbitrary and made the free tier look stingier than it is. At ten cents the same tapes cost 16 and 46. MARGINS ARE UNCHANGED -- every plan's creditsPerPeriod was rescaled in the same edit, so each plan buys exactly the number of tapes it bought before. This is the honest way to make the numbers friendlier: scale the unit, do not discount the tape. Selling 720p at '100 credits' while it costs 152 credits' worth of provider time would have been a 52-credit loss on every render, invisible until an invoice arrived.
_referenceSeconds_comment: The duration every estimatedUSDPer15s below is quoted at, and not a default so much as the contract: 375 frames at 25fps, asserted by ~200 tests. `creditCost` scales linearly from here for any other duration.

provider._comment: ESTIMATE, and PROVENANCE rather than the engine: `creditCost` computes from the estimatedUSDPer15s figures below, not from these fields. They are here because the 720p figure was derived from fal's published video token formula -- tokens = height * width * seconds * 24 / 1024, billed at $0.014 per 1000 tokens -- and a number whose derivation is not written down becomes folklore in about a month. A test asserts that the 720p estimate still matches this formula, so an edit that breaks the link is caught rather than absorbed. The 480p and 1080p figures are NOT this formula: pixel count is not the whole rate, because fal's fast Seedance tier tops out at 720p and the tiers are priced differently.
provider.source: fal published token formula, no invoice yet, UNVERIFIED

480p._comment:
ESTIMATE, and the cheap tier. 640x480 through the token formula is 108000 tokens, $1.51 for 15 seconds. CORRECTED 2026-08-20: this entry previously recorded 854x480 while carrying the $1.51 price, and those two disagree -- 854x480 is $2.02. The dimensions were the 16:9 shape of "480p", but THIS PRODUCT ALWAYS REQUESTS 4:3, so 640x480 is the raster and $1.51 is the matching number. Recording a price derived one way beside dimensions derived another is how an estimate quietly becomes unfalsifiable. THE NON-OBVIOUS RISK, and it is a real one: 480 is BELOW the tape raster vertically (the tape works at 736x588 per config/render.json), so this is the only option that is upscaled before the grain goes on, and the only one that actually loses detail. That loss is invisible on a test pattern. It is UNTESTED ON A FACE, and likeness is the entire product. A legitimate cheap tier, not a free lunch.

ANSWERED 2026-08-24 BY A REAL INVOICE, and the answer is the expensive one: FAL BILLS THE RASTER IT RETURNS, NOT THE ONE YOU ORDER. Two direct jobs ordered 640x480 and were delivered 752x560; fal's usage page charged 296.92k tokens at $0.014/1k = $4.156908, which is exactly w*h*seconds*24/1024 computed on the DELIVERED size. The formula in `provider` above is therefore CORRECT and was never the problem. What is wrong is the assumption that ordering a raster gets you that raster. For this tier specifically: 640x480 x 15s is 108000 tokens and $1.5120, but the two jobs that actually ran cost $2.0785 each -- a 37.5% surcharge caused entirely by the model returning a bigger frame than it was asked for. `estimatedUSDPer15s` BELOW IS DELIBERATELY UNCHANGED: it feeds `creditCost`, so editing it changes what a customer is charged, and that is Paul's decision and not a bookkeeping one. But it is now KNOWN to understate real cost by about a third, which is the unsafe direction -- this file's own header says overstating cost is the safe way to be wrong. Either the raster gets honoured (config/models.json, aspect ratios) or this number goes up.
480p._raster_comment: WHAT THE RENDERER ACTUALLY ASKS FOR. Identical to width/height here, because the price above was already derived at the 4:3 raster. See the 720p row, where they differ, for why the field exists at all.
480p.source: provider formula at the 4:3 raster we actually request, UNVERIFIED

720p._comment:
ESTIMATE, and the anchor: 1280x720 through the token formula above is 324000 tokens, $4.54 for 15 seconds. It is also the resolution the product is designed around. The tape works at 736x588 (720x576 plus jitter headroom), and 720p is the first size that fully covers that raster -- which makes it the last size that buys anything. Measured SSIM between a 720p-sourced and a 1080p-sourced delivery was 0.958 and the two are indistinguishable at 4x zoom. OPEN QUESTION, and it is worth a metered call rather than an argument: this anchor uses 1280x720, the 16:9 shape. We request 4:3, and 960x720 through the same formula is $3.40, not $4.54. Whether the provider bills the raster it renders or the nominal frame size is not documented anywhere we could find. The higher figure is kept deliberately -- overstating cost understates margin, which is the safe direction to be wrong in. Do NOT lower it to $3.40 on reasoning alone; one --meter run settles it.

ANSWERED 2026-08-24 BY A REAL INVOICE, and the answer is the expensive one: FAL BILLS THE RASTER IT RETURNS, NOT THE ONE YOU ORDER. Two direct jobs ordered 640x480 and were delivered 752x560; fal's usage page charged 296.92k tokens at $0.014/1k = $4.156908, which is exactly w*h*seconds*24/1024 computed on the DELIVERED size. The formula in `provider` above is therefore CORRECT and was never the problem. What is wrong is the assumption that ordering a raster gets you that raster. That settles the open question this entry raised: it does NOT bill the 4:3 raster we request, and it does not reliably send it either. The $3.40-versus-$4.54 argument recorded above cannot be resolved from the request side at all -- only from what comes back. UNMETERED at this tier: no 720p job has ever run.
720p._raster_comment: WHAT THE RENDERER ACTUALLY ASKS FOR, and it is NOT width/height above. THIS PRODUCT ALWAYS REQUESTS 4:3 -- the tape raster is 720x576 at SAR 16/15, i.e. DAR 4:3 -- so `720p` means 960x720 on the wire and nothing ever renders 1280x720. The two fields disagree on purpose and each is honest about a different thing: `raster` is the picture, `width`/`height` are the shape the PRICE above was derived at, and the open question in the _comment is exactly whether fal bills the raster it renders or the nominal frame. The higher figure is kept until a --meter run settles it. scripts/animate/plan.mjs derives the raster from the label (the number is the height, 4:3 gives the width) and scripts/providers/fal.mjs derives the same two rasters for its own resolution enum; a test asserts all three agree, so this row cannot drift away from what is requested without something going red.

1080p._comment: DEFERRED, NOT CANCELLED, and the row is kept with its reasoning attached so that turning it on later is a one-field change rather than an archaeology exercise -- and so nobody re-derives the same measurement in six months. Why it is off: roughly 2.25x the cost of 720p for pixels that are thrown away before the grain is applied, because the tape raster is 736x588 and 720p already covers it (SSIM 0.958 against a 1080p source, indistinguishable at 4x zoom). It also forces the expensive standard tier, since fal's fast Seedance tops out at 720p -- so it is more than 2.25x the cost in practice. Set `available: true` when there is a reason; `creditCost` refuses it until then rather than quietly rendering something else.
1080p._raster_comment: Recorded for the same reason the rest of this row is: turning 1080p on later should be a field, not an archaeology exercise. Nothing may request it while `available` is false -- creditCost throws, and so does resolutionRaster in scripts/animate/plan.mjs.

standard._comment: Not an estimate: a multiplier of exactly 1 is the identity, and it is listed rather than special-cased so the tier seam is exercised end to end before a second tier exists. A faster or higher-quality tier is one entry here plus one MEASURED multiplier. Do NOT add a speculative second tier -- an invented multiplier in the money path is a guess that bills somebody.

defaults._comment: What the estimate on the Record button is computed with when nothing else is asked for. 480p is the default because it is the cheap tier and the product is credit-conscious; 720p is the one that is worth paying for, and the page should say so.

packs._comment:
WHAT IS SOLD. A one-off bundle of credits, bought through Stripe Checkout, granted by a signature-verified webhook and by nothing else. Specified in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-24-credit-packs-pricing-design.md, which SUPERSEDED the subscription model on 2026-08-24 for two measured reasons: a tape costs $2.08 rather than $1.51 (fal bills tokens, and bills the raster it RETURNS), and the usage pattern is bursty -- three tapes in one evening and nothing for six months -- which a monthly subscription bills badly and cannot measure. A pack also answers the one question a subscription cannot: renewal is inertia, repurchase is a choice.

THE PRICE A CUSTOMER PAYS IS THE STRIPE PRICE, NOT priceUSD. `priceUSD` below is what this repo believes the Price says, and it is what the page prints and what the margin assertion in test/billing-packs.test.js checks. Stripe charges what the Price object says and nothing else -- there is no amount, no currency and no price_data anywhere in the checkout request, deliberately, so nothing a browser sends can change what is charged. If the two ever disagree, the Price is right and this file is stale.

NOTHING CAN BE BOUGHT WHILE stripePriceId IS null. A Price is immutable in Stripe, so creating one is the LAST step and it is gated on section 7 of the spec: meter the parked 720p job, fix the estimator so --dry-run can tell 480p from 720p, and run the blind check. Until then POST /api/billing/checkout answers 503 and the button on /pricing is disabled with a sentence saying why.

starter._comment:
ESTIMATE IN ONE DIRECTION ONLY. $10 and 40 CR are the spec's decision (section 2.3) rather than a guess, but WHAT 40 CREDITS BUYS IS STILL MOVING. The spec sizes this pack against a REPRICED tape -- 21 CR at 480p, derived from the measured $2.0785 at a cost basis of $0.10 a credit -- so "$10 buys one tape, with 19 CR left over" is true AT THAT PRICE. The resolutions block above still says 16 CR, because editing estimatedUSDPer15s changes what a customer is charged and that is Paul's decision, gated on the same section 7 that gates the Price. So TODAY 40 CR buys two 480p tapes rather than one, and no 720p tape at all (46 CR). That is safe, because nothing can be sold until a Price exists. It is written down because the two numbers have to move in the SAME edit and not months apart.

MARGIN, at the spec's numbers: 40 CR for $10 is $0.25 a credit against a $0.10 cost basis -- 2.5x, 60% gross before Stripe's cut and about 64% after it on the worst-case single-tape spend. $0.25 rather than $0.20 is a decision about FREE RETRIES and not about the spreadsheet: direct mode deleted the cheap rejection gate, so a bad likeness now costs a whole tape and the customer finds out after the money is spent. Tapes will be regenerated for nothing. $0.25 absorbs one regenerate in six; $0.20 does not.

EXPIRY IS NOT SET AND THAT IS DELIBERATE. Section 2.4 of the spec recommends twelve months and section 9 lists it as open and needing Paul. `grant.expiryDays` below is still null, so these credits do not expire -- and it must stay null until something actually WRITES the negative ledger row that realises an expiry, because a date shown to a customer that no code enforces is worse than no date at all.
starter.label: Forty credits
starter.source: spec section 2.3, approved 2026-08-24; the Stripe Price does not exist yet

grant._comment: ESTIMATE in the sense that the cadence is a product decision nobody has taken yet. periodDays is the interval a plan's creditsPerPeriod is granted on. expiryDays is null, which means CREDITS DO NOT EXPIRE and the balance simply accumulates; if Paul decides they should not roll over, set it and realise the expiry as an explicit negative ledger entry, never as a silent adjustment -- credits vanishing without a ledger line is precisely the unauditable thing the ledger exists to prevent. DECISION NEEDED.

free._comment: ESTIMATE. 16 credits is exactly one 480p tape (rescaled from 51 when creditUSD moved to $0.10; same one tape), which keeps the previously specified 'free: 1 tape per month' true under the credit mechanism. It is not enough for a 720p tape, and that is the shape of the free tier rather than an oversight. Zero is the only price in this file that cannot drift.
free.label: Free

shelf._comment: ESTIMATE. 48 credits is exactly three 480p tapes (rescaled from 153; same three tapes), preserving the allowance the flat spec named -- or one 720p tape with a 480p one left over, which is the trade the credit model exists to let a person make. $10/month against $4.53 of estimated provider spend at full 480p usage is a 55% gross margin BEFORE any infrastructure; at full 720p usage it is 55% of one tape and then nothing, which is the correct behaviour and not a bug. annualUSD is ten months for twelve -- an interpretation of Paul's 'price it very small annually', not his words. NEEDS PAUL.
shelf.label: Shelf

archive._comment: ESTIMATE. 64 credits is exactly four 480p tapes (rescaled from 204; same four tapes), or one 720p tape plus one 480p. $12/month against $6.04 of estimated provider spend is a 50% gross margin; the annual rate at $10/month effective is 40%. The ladder is still weak on its own terms: two dollars and 51 credits apart is one extra 480p tape a month, which has to read as obviously worth two dollars or it looks like indecision. Flagged in docs/interfaces-app.md, unchanged by the move to credits, and worth revisiting the moment a --meter run gives these numbers a floor.
archive.label: Archive
